title: Noach: ten generations of waiting (Avot 5:2)
hook: from Noah to Abraham ten generations pass with no one turning

segments.voice: Yesterday, two sons walking backward with a cloak, covering their father without looking. Your line was walk backward with the cloak. Today, the last day of the portion of Noah. Day one hundred seventy.

Some changes move slower than a lifetime. A habit that won't break. A family pattern that shows up in the grandparents, then the parents, then the kids. A cause that moves an inch a decade. After long enough, it starts to sound like this: if it hasn't changed by now, it never will. The end of the portion of Noah is mostly lists of names. Nations, cities, a tower that never gets finished, then more names. It's easy to skim. But a teaching in Pirkei Avot counts those names, and finds something in them about waiting. Today.
screen: `SLOWER THAN A LIFETIME.` → `LISTS OF NAMES, EASY TO SKIM.` → `PIRKEI AVOT COUNTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Pirkei Avot says: there were ten generations from Adam to Noah, to show how patient God is. All those generations kept provoking God, until God brought the flood. Then: there were ten generations from Noah to Abraham, to show how patient God is. All those generations kept provoking God, until Abraham came and received the reward of them all. Ten generations, twice over. That is a long wait for one person to turn. And look how the two lists end differently. The first ten generations end in a flood. The second ten end in Abraham. Same patience, different ending. What changed? Someone finally turned. The portion itself shows you the waiting. After the flood, people build a city and a tower to reach the heavens, to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them. Then come the names again. And at the very end of the portion, a small detail. Abraham's father, Terah, takes his family and sets out from Ur toward the land of Canaan. And they get as far as Haran, and stop, and settle there. Terah dies in Haran. He was headed in the right direction, and didn't arrive. The next portion begins with his son picking up the road. So this portion ends in the middle of a journey. That's what a slow change looks like in this telling. Generation after generation, and nothing. A father who starts and stops. And then a son who keeps going.
screen: `TEN GENERATIONS FROM ADAM TO NOAH.` · `TEN MORE, UNTIL ABRAHAM CAME.` · `A TOWER, AND MORE NAMES.` · `TERAH SETS OUT, AND STOPS IN HARAN.` · then, large: `TEN GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with a slow change. Settle, and breathe. Think of one change you've been waiting for, in yourself or in someone you love. Notice the impatience: the sigh, the it'll never happen. Let it be there. Then remember the ten generations, and Terah stopping in Haran, and his son picking up the road. Maybe you're the one who starts. Maybe you're the one who keeps going. Either way, the road isn't wasted. The bell holds the time.
Noach. The portion of Noah: a whole-hearted man, a window, laws for everyone, a cloak, and ten generations of waiting.
Your line: ten generations. Today, do one small thing toward a slow change, without needing to see the end. Tomorrow, the road picks up again. Day one hundred seventy.

screen: `DAY 170 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LECH LECHA: GO TO YOURSELF.`

howItsDone: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons; its fifth chapter's teachings on the ten generations are read alongside the genealogies at the end of the portion of Noach.

fork.setup: you're Terah. you've set out from Ur with your family, headed for Canaan. you reach Haran. what does the Torah say you do?
fork.reveal: Terah settles in Haran and dies there. the next portion begins with his son picking up the road.

original.note: Hebrew: generations; the singular is dor.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the portion is just lists of names.
what it means: the lists count ten generations of waiting, and end with a father who starts toward Canaan and stops.
what a scholar hears: Avot 5:2 on the two sets of ten generations; Genesis 11:31–32, Terah in Haran; the Babel story (11:1–9) in between.

notes: Avot 5:2 paraphrased closely; confirm wording ('received the reward of them all').
'Roughly as far from us as the 1700s' assumes 25–30 years a generation (250–300 years); confirm or drop.
Terah setting out from Ur toward Canaan and dying in Haran (11:31–32): confirm. The script does not retell the midrash of Abraham and the idols.

Editor review (days 170–187): hook reopened (was 'Think about…'); cut the unsourced 'twenty-five or thirty years a generation… the 1700s' arithmetic and the 'nine generations… in the tenth' count, which Avot 5:2 does not state that way.
